answer.evidence: The roof is a sloped plane of door panels in four colors across rows 0-15. It ends in a brown edge line at row 15, with a dark eave shadow at row 16. Below it the front wall runs rows 17-46. The wall is stacked pallets with a plank lintel at rows 17-19 and a dark entrance gap at rows 21-46. The sack sits inside the entrance and counts as decor. The roof is a clear top surface of 16 rows above a front face of about 30 rows, so it reads as three-quarter view.

styleAnswer.evidence: The candidate is a small building, about 2.5 tiles wide, and it is much simpler than the references. Its measured facts are close to theirs: 9 visible tones per tile against 12 and 10, 7% near-flat coverage, and 0% neutral dark edges, so the outlines are tinted and not a black sticker line. By eye, each material has only about 2-3 steps. The door panels on the roof are a base tone with a light edge and a dark seam, with none of the per-tile highlights and scalloped tile shading of the references. The pallet wall has some slat and grain variation, but it is regular and shallow. The dark entrance and the sack are readable. The piece is cleanly drawn but flatter and thinner than the references, which carry 5-6 shading steps per material. Because the shading is shallow, I fail it.
